citeAs: Talmor, A., Herzig, J., Lourie, N., and Berant, J. (2019). CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge. arXiv:1811.00937.
creator: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, Jonathan Berant (Tel-Aviv University; Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence)
description: CommonsenseQA is a multiple-choice question answering dataset of 12,247 questions designed to test commonsense knowledge. Questions are generated by crowd workers who observe source and target concepts from ConceptNet and author questions that require background knowledge to discriminate between semantically similar answer candidates. Each question has five candidate answers (one correct, four distractors).
name: CommonsenseQA
publisher: Tel-Aviv University; Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
rai:annotatorDemographics: 122 crowd workers contributed to question generation; 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions. A separate disjoint group of workers performed verification. Human evaluation used workers not involved in question generation, with no qualification test or AMT master worker requirement.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions verified by at least one of two workers answering correctly were retained; this process filtered out 15% of questions. Human accuracy on 100 sampled questions was 88.9% (majority vote from 5 workers).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: AMT workers were shown a question concept and three answer concepts, and asked to formulate three questions (one per target concept) such that each question has one correct answer and the other two targets are distractors. Workers were instructed to avoid surface clues (e.g., not to use the word 'open' when the answer is 'door'). Workers also added two additional distractors per question (one from ConceptNet, one manually authored). A separate group of workers verified questions by annotating them as unanswerable or choosing the correct answer. Only workers with at least 75% question pass rate were accepted.
rai:dataBiases: The paper acknowledges annotation artifacts as a known issue in commonsense datasets, noting that distributional biases can allow models to achieve high performance without true understanding. The dataset design specifically addresses this by using semantically similar distractors (sharing the same ConceptNet relation) to prevent models from using simple surface clues. Workers were instructed to avoid surface clues. Analysis found that 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions, indicating skewed contributor distribution.
rai:dataCollection: Questions were generated by Amazon Mechanical Turk crowd workers who observed source and target concepts from ConceptNet and authored multiple-choice questions. Workers were asked to formulate three questions per subgraph (one per target concept), add two additional distractors per question, and verify question quality. A separate group of workers verified question quality. Web snippets from Google search were also collected as textual context for each question.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet knowledge base subgraphs, consisting of triplets (concept, relation, concept). The paper uses 236,208 filtered triplets from ConceptNet's 32 million total triplets, organized into approximately 43,000 question sets.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered by: (1) removing general or well-explored relations (e.g., RelatedTo, IsA), keeping 22 relations; (2) removing triplets where a concept is more than four words or not in English; (3) removing triplets where edit distance between source and target concepts is too low. Questions failing verification (15%) were removed. The dataset was split 80/10/10 into train/dev/test sets.
rai:dataUseCases: Evaluating commonsense question answering systems; benchmarking NLU models on commonsense knowledge; investigating the incorporation of commonsense knowledge into NLU systems.

evidence.name: we present COMMONSENSE QA: a challenging new dataset for commonsense question answering.
evidence.description: We create 12,247 questions through this procedure and demonstrate the difficulty of our task with a large number of strong baselines. Our best baseline is based on BERT-large (Devlin et al., 2018) and obtains 56% accuracy, well below human performance, which is 89%.
evidence.url: The dataset can be downloaded from www.tau-nlp.org/commonsenseqa . The code for all our baselines is available at github.com/jonathanherzig/commonsenseqa .

evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers to generate and validate commonsense questions. We issue a web query to Google search for every question and candidate answer, concatenating the answer to the question. We extract subgraphs from CONCEPTNET, each with one source concept and three target concepts.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: CONCEPTNET is a graph knowledge-base GCRC, where the nodes C represent natural language concepts, and edges R represent commonsense relations. CONCEPTNET contains 32 million triplets. This results in a set of 236,208 triplets (q; r; a), where we call the first concept the question concept and the second concept the answer concept.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers to generate and validate commonsense questions.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: AMT workers saw, for every question set, the question concept and three answer concepts. They were asked to formulate three questions, where all questions contain the question concept. Each question should have as an answer one of the answer concepts, but not the other two. To discourage workers from providing simple surface clues for the answer, they were instructed to avoid using words that have a strong relation to the answer concept, for example, not to use the word 'open' when the answer is 'door'.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each question is verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly are used.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each question is verified by 2 workers, and only questions verified by at least one worker that answered correctly are used. This processes filters out 15% of the questions.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We filter triplets with general relations (e.g., RelatedTo) or relations that are already well-explored in NLP (e.g., IsA). In total we use 22 relations. We filter triplets where one of the concepts is more than four words or not in English. We filter triplets where the edit distance between c1 and c2 is too low.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Investigations of commonsense datasets, and of natural language datasets more generally, have revealed the difficulty in creating benchmarks that measure the understanding of a program rather than its ability to take advantage of distributional biases, and to model the annotation process. To discourage workers from providing simple surface clues for the answer, they were instructed to avoid using words that have a strong relation to the answer concept.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: We hope that this dataset facilitates future work in incorporating commonsense knowledge into NLU systems.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: This type of knowledge seems trivial for humans, but is still out of the reach of current natural language understanding (NLU) systems. We hope that this dataset facilitates future work in incorporating commonsense knowledge into NLU systems.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: 122 formulators contributed to question generation. However, 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions. To test human accuracy, we created a separate task for which we did not use a qualification test, nor used AMT master workers.
